name: Veet depilatory cream

card.summary: Chemical hair-dissolving cream from Reckitt: fast, painless-at-the-surface hair removal that regrows in days.
card.note: Alkaline thioglycolate chemistry can irritate skin; patch-test guidance appears on labels.

quick.overview:
Veet is a mass-market depilatory brand. Its creams dissolve the hair shaft chemically so hair can be wiped away at the skin surface, as an alternative to shaving or waxing.

Hair regrows because the follicle is not affected, and no clinical trials of the creams were found.
quick.mechanism: Thioglycolate salts in a high-pH base break the disulfide bonds in hair keratin, softening the shaft until it can be wiped off.
quick.risks: Irritation and chemical burns are possible with alkaline depilatories; a 2002 case series linked Veet wax strips (not creams) to allergic contact dermatitis. Labels advise patch testing.

lead: Veet is a brand of chemical depilatory creams, lotions and gels that give a smooth, hair-free look on legs, underarms, bikini line, face and men's body hair by dissolving the keratin of the hair shaft so it can be wiped off at the skin surface. People use it to remove hair quickly at home without a razor or wax; it is owned by Reckitt Benckiser and traces its origin to a Canadian product sold under the name Neet from 1919.[1][2]

The active chemistry is the same family used across the depilatory category: thioglycolate salts in an alkaline base that break the disulfide bonds in keratin.[2][3] Because the hair is cut below the skin surface but the follicle is left intact, hair regrows; Wikipedia notes depilatories do not destroy the dermal papilla.[3]

No clinical trials of Veet creams for appearance outcomes are indexed. The published literature on the brand consists mainly of a dermatology report of allergic contact dermatitis linked to Veet wax-strip products, which are a different product type from the creams.[4]

paras: Veet products are sold as tube creams, jar lotions, gels, sprays and wax strips for legs, underarms, bikini line and face, with variants for sensitive or dry skin and for men.[1][2] Marketing materials describe application times of a few minutes before the dissolved hair is wiped away.[1]

According to the manufacturer, thioglycolic acid and potassium hydroxide react to form potassium thioglycolate, which breaks keratin's disulfide bonds and weakens the hair.[2] Depilatory creams in general contain roughly 5-6 percent calcium thioglycolate in a high-pH base, a mixture that hydrolyses hair but is also irritating to skin if left on too long.[3]

Wikipedia's depilatory article lists the active ingredients as salts of thioglycolic and thiolactic acid, which break the bonds that hold keratin together and partly hydrolyse the hair so it lifts away. Calcium or strontium hydroxide keeps the pH near 12, and older sulfide-based products such as strontium sulfide were replaced by thiols because of their smell.[3] Hair destruction takes about ten minutes in the encyclopedia account, after which the area is rinsed carefully; the product label governs actual timing.[3]

The product originated as Neet, trademarked in Canada by the Hannibal Pharmacal Company in 1918-1919, with a US trademark granted in 1922.[2] The Veet name was established in the UK in 1922, and Canada and the US continued to use Neet until 2002.[2] Reckitt & Colman acquired the trademark in 1990 according to Wikipedia, while Grokipedia gives a 1969 acquisition date; the two sources disagree.[1][2] A 2022 reformulation range, Veet Pure, is described by Grokipedia as using plant extracts to reduce irritation.[1]

Depilatory chemistry is older than the brand. Wikipedia notes that Greek and Roman writers described depilatory ointments and plasters called psilothrum, and that Jewish legend credits King Solomon with a depilatory made from lime, water and orpiment (arsenic trisulfide).[3] Product ranges later expanded beyond creams into wax strips; Grokipedia reports ready-to-use strips were introduced in India in 2009.[1]

Veet sells variants for sensitive, normal and dry skin and for men, and for legs, underarms, bikini line, face and body, with application times of roughly 3 to 6 minutes according to the manufacturer's descriptions summarised by Grokipedia.[1] Because depilation cuts hair below the skin surface without removing the follicle, regrowth occurs; the dermal papilla is not destroyed.[3] Depilatories sit alongside shaving and waxing as options for temporary hair removal.[3]

A 2002 report in Contact Dermatitis described 33 cases of acute allergic contact dermatitis in France and Belgium linked to Veet epilating waxes and their accompanying tissue; some were severe enough to require hospitalisation or systemic corticosteroids, and sensitisation sometimes occurred after the first use.[4] The report concerned wax products rather than depilatory creams.

Product labels generally advise patch testing and keeping the cream off broken or irritated skin; such label guidance is attributed to manufacturers and is not an independent finding. Because the chemistry is alkaline, the depilatory article notes that rinsing and applying conditioners afterwards returns skin to its normal pH.[3]

Early advertising presented Neet as a faster alternative to shaving.[2] Wikipedia records that a 2014 Veet advertising campaign drew criticism for portraying unshaven women as masculine, and that one ad was withdrawn after complaints it was homophobic and transphobic; a 2011 French promotional site was also removed after complaints.[2]
No studies found. The nearest published research is a 2002 case series of allergic reactions to Veet wax products, not a trial of the cream.[4]

timeline.event: US trademark granted; Veet name established in the UK.[2]
Reckitt & Colman acquires the trademark (per Wikipedia).[2]
Neet name retired in Canada and the US in favour of Veet.[2]

angle.text: The cream removes visible hair at the skin surface in a few minutes, leaving a smooth finish that lasts until the hair regrows. People use it on legs, underarms and body areas where they want less visible hair.
